behavior_items: The reproducer defines a minimal span-like view type `MySpan<T>` that stores a raw pointer `data_` and a length `size_`. It does not own storage; it is only a lightweight view over an existing array.
`MySpan::operator[]` returns `T&` by indexing the stored pointer, so the returned reference designates the original array element, not a subobject inside the `MySpan` object itself.
`make_my_span` takes an array by reference `T const(&x)[n]`, so the function parameter refers directly to the caller's array and no array temporary is created.

Inside `make_my_span`, `std::begin(x)` yields a pointer to the first element of the caller-provided array. The returned `MySpan<T const>` therefore contains a pointer into the still-alive array object from `main`.
In `main`, `x` is a local array with automatic storage duration that remains alive until the end of `main`, so any pointer or reference to `x[0]` is valid for the whole scope after construction.

The expression `make_my_span(x)[0]` first creates a temporary `MySpan` prvalue, then immediately invokes `operator[]` on that temporary. Even though the view object is temporary, `operator[]` returns a reference to `x[0]`, whose lifetime is independent of the temporary view.
Binding `int const& y{make_my_span(x)[0]};` is therefore semantically safe: `y` refers to `x[0]`, not to storage owned by or embedded in the temporary `MySpan` object.

The reproducer compares this with `std::span` via `make_span`, which performs the same conceptual operation: construct a non-owning view over `x` and return a reference to an element through `operator[]`.

GCC accepts the `std::span` case but warns for the custom `MySpan` case under `-Wdangling-reference`, showing that the warning logic special-cases or better understands the standard library type but not equivalent user-defined span-like types.

The warning is a false positive because the compiler appears to reason that a reference obtained from indexing a temporary object may dangle when the temporary expires, without proving that the returned reference aliases external storage reachable through the stored pointer.

The important lifetime distinction exercised by the reproducer is 'temporary view object' versus 'lifetime of the data being viewed'. Destroying the temporary `MySpan` does not invalidate the referenced array element because `MySpan` is non-owning.

The bug report also notes the same warning appears for both const and non-const references, indicating the issue is not cv-qualification but the escape/lifetime analysis performed for references returned from user-defined proxy/view types.

This test stresses GCC's static analysis for `-Wdangling-reference` on user-defined classes that mimic `std::span` semantics: a constructor from pointer+size, immediate indexing on a temporary, and reference binding to the indexed result.

The reproducer is especially targeted because the standard-library analogue compiles cleanly, so the observed behavior demonstrates inconsistent compiler treatment of semantically equivalent code paths rather than an actual program lifetime bug.
test_behavior_analysis.summary: The code constructs a non-owning span-like object over a real array and immediately indexes that temporary view to bind a reference to an array element. The temporary `MySpan` dies at the end of the full expression, but the referenced element belongs to `x`, whose lifetime continues, so the reference is valid. GCC's `-Wdangling-reference` incorrectly warns for the custom span-like class while not warning for equivalent `std::span` code, showing a false positive caused by incomplete lifetime reasoning for user-defined non-owning view types.

test_failure_analysis.analysis: The failure pattern is a false positive from GCC's C++ front-end lifetime analysis for -Wdangling-reference. The common structure is: a temporary non-owning view object is returned by value, an element access member function is invoked immediately on that temporary, and the member returns T& referring to external storage reached through an internal pointer field. GCC warns for the user-defined span-like class but not for semantically equivalent std::span code, so the bug is likely in warning-generation logic that ties the returned reference lifetime too closely to the temporary base object instead of tracing that the reference ultimately aliases the caller's array. Because the array is passed by reference into make_my_span and remains alive in main, the reference cannot actually dangle. This points to incomplete or overly conservative handling of user-defined view/proxy types, especially around operator[] on temporaries, prvalue materialization, and propagation of pointee lifetime through constructors and data members.
possible_causes: Missing or overly narrow modeling in -Wdangling-reference for user-defined non-owning view types: GCC likely recognizes std::span specially, but fails to generalize equivalent semantics for custom classes storing a pointer and returning references through operator[].

Incorrect lifetime propagation through member access on temporaries: the warning logic may assume that a reference returned from calling operator[] on a temporary object depends on the temporary object's lifetime, instead of distinguishing references to external pointee storage from references to the object's own subobjects.

Failure in alias/pointee analysis across constructor initialization and return-by-value: GCC may not connect MySpan::data_ back to the original array argument passed by reference into make_my_span, so it conservatively treats the result of data_[idx] as derived from a soon-to-die temporary.

Over-conservative handling of prvalue temporary materialization in the C++ front end: make_my_span(x)[0] may be classified like access through a temporary container whose destruction invalidates references, without checking that the type is non-owning and trivially destructible with no lifetime effect on pointees.

Defect in warning heuristics for reference-returning member functions of user-defined classes: GCC may lack interprocedural reasoning that operator[] simply dereferences a stored pointer, causing a false dangling diagnosis whenever such a function is invoked on a temporary object.

Inconsistent standard-library special-casing versus generic analysis: std::span likely bypasses or augments the generic dangling-reference warning path, while MySpan follows the generic path and is misdiagnosed, indicating a defect in the generic implementation rather than in the reproducer.
evidence: MySpan stores only T* and size, so it is a non-owning view; destroying the temporary MySpan does not destroy or invalidate the underlying array.
MySpan::operator[] returns T& via data_[idx], which refers to the original array element rather than to storage inside the MySpan object.
make_my_span takes the array as T const(&x)[n], meaning the function receives a reference to the caller's array and no temporary array is created.
std::begin(x) in make_my_span yields a pointer into the caller's still-live array, so the returned MySpan contains a pointer with valid lifetime in main.
In main, x lives to the end of scope, so binding int const& y to x[0] through the temporary view is semantically safe.
The expression make_my_span(x)[0] warns, but the equivalent make_span(x)[0] using std::span does not, demonstrating inconsistent compiler treatment of equivalent lifetime behavior.
The bug report states the warning appears for both const and non-const references, which supports that the root issue is lifetime/alias analysis rather than cv-qualification semantics.

The reproducer specifically exercises immediate indexing on a temporary returned-by-value view object, matching a likely weak spot in GCC's dangling-reference analysis for user-defined proxy/view classes.

If FLAGS is LOOKUP_ONLYCONVERTING then it is the = init form of the initializer, if FLAGS is 0, then it is the (init) form. If INIT resolves to a CALL_EXPR which happens to return something of the type we are looking for, then we know that we can safely use that call to perform the initialization. The virtual function table pointer cannot be set up here, because we do not really know its type. This never calls operator=(). When initializing, nothing is CONST. A default copy constructor may have to be used to perform the initialization. A constructor or a conversion operator may have to be used to perform the initialization, but not both, as it would be ambiguous.

In this case, it may be EXP, or may just contain EXP. The reason we need this is because if EXP is a base element of TRUE_EXP, we don't necessarily know by looking at EXP where its virtual baseclass fields should really be pointing.
